what_its_for: Dostarlimab-Gxly is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including endometrial cancer (cancer of the lining of the uterus) and other solid tumors that have a specific genetic change called mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR). It works by helping your immune system find and attack cancer cells.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV infusion (a drip into your vein) by a nurse or doctor at a clinic or hospital. Each infusion takes about 30 minutes. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Your healthcare team will schedule your appointments and monitor you closely during and after each infusion.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your treatment plan and the type of cancer being treated. A common schedule is one infusion every 3 weeks for the first 4 doses, then one infusion every 6 weeks after that. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your schedule may be different.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given at a clinic, your healthcare team will help schedule all your appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away. Do not skip doses without talking to your doctor first, as keeping your treatment schedule is very important for the medicine to work properly.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. If for any reason you are given a supply to take somewhere, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C), do not freeze it, and keep it in the original container away from light.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine or yellow fever vaccine) while being treated with this medicine without checking with your doctor first. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, as some may interact with this treatment. Avoid activities that could increase infection risk, and let your doctor know right away if you feel unwell.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following, as they could be signs of serious immune system reactions: rash, blisters, or peeling skin; chest pain, shortness of breath, or irregular heartbeat; severe stomach pain, diarrhea, or blood in your stool; dark urine, yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); unusual headaches, dizziness, or vision changes; muscle weakness or numbness; pain or difficulty urinating; swelling in your legs or body; fever or chills. These side effects can happen during treatment or even weeks to months after your last dose.
when_it_works: Every patient is different, and it may take several weeks or months before you notice improvement. Your doctor will do regular tests and scans to check how well the medicine is working. Do not stop treatment on your own even if you do not feel immediate changes, as the medicine may still be working inside your body.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. It can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 4 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 4 months after the last dose, as the medicine may pass into breast milk and harm a nursing baby. Older adults: This medicine has been used safely in older adults, but you may be monitored more closely for side effects. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
